inlines.text: 4.1.6 言语化的元博弈与监督博弈

blocks.text: 言语化元博弈是指模型在思维链（CoT）中推理自己将如何被评分、奖励或监控，而不是只专注于既定任务。我们报告这一指标，是因为它会影响对观察到的行为的解读：例如，观察到的对齐行为可能并不反映真正的对齐；反过来，粗心的行为也可能是模型误以为自己身处玩具环境所致。模型表现出言语化元博弈的评估，可以像受污染的评估（即模型在训练中见过的评估）一样对待。测量这一指标有助于我们了解评估与监督结果是否反映了我们想要测量的行为。

inlines.text: 2.1.2.2.1 Sandbox Bench

blocks.text: Sandbox Bench is an internal OpenAI evaluation that tests whether a model can find and exploit vulnerabilities in software components similar to those we use in our infrastructure. The targets include runtimes, file parsers, and proxies that control outbound network traffic.

is an internal OpenAI evaluation that tests whether a model can find and exploit vulnerabilities in software components similar to those we use in our infrastructure. The targets include runtimes, file parsers, and proxies that control outbound network traffic.

blocks.text: For each target, the model receives the component’s source code and its dependencies, along with an isolated environment where it can run the software. A target counts as solved when the model exploits a flaw to retrieve a protected secret, called a flag. For example, a model might exploit a flaw in a file parser while the parser remains confined to a virtual machine. We use the results to gauge the complexity of the vulnerabilities models can exploit and to identify which components could benefit from hardening. In production, containers, operating systems, and hardened virtual machines provide additional layers of isolation for runtimes. A sandbox escape would require getting past those layers as well.

blocks.text: 2.2.1.1 Biological and Chemical Threat Modeling

inlines.text: 2.2.1.1 Biological and Chemical Threat Modeling

blocks.text: We assess biological and chemical security risk at both the High capability level (novice pursuing a known pathogen) and the Critical capability level (expert pursuing a novel pathogen). Our threat models focus on how AI may provide meaningful counterfactual uplift when viewed across a full biological/chemical threat pathway, focusing on the key bottlenecks identified by subject-matter experts as well as how these bottlenecks might differ across different threat actors like lone wolves, non-state groups, state programs, insider risks, and autonomous agents.

blocks.text: At our High threshold, the primary pathway we anticipate threat actors will try to use AI models to cause severe harm is via persistent probing for dual-use biological and chemical content. As a result, our safeguards approach has focused on proactively preventing such content via a multilayered defense stack. We are less concerned about a single model response bypassing one defensive layer because we hypothesize that a threat actor would likely need repeated, tailored troubleshooting across multiple steps to succeed. Thus, currently, we rely on refusals, blocks, and bans to prevent severe harm in our General Access products.

inlines.text: 2.2.2.2 Cybersecurity Safety Training and Evaluation

blocks.text: We train GPT-6.2 Astra and GPT-6.2 Sol to safely refuse prohibited cybersecurity assistance while preserving useful help on legitimate defensive cybersecurity work. In initial model-level evaluations, GPT-6.2 Astra and Sol both refused fewer harmless requests than GPT-6 Astra, but both models were also less resistant to jailbreaks than GPT-6 Astra. In response, we adjusted the refusal boundary to make both GPT-6.2 models more conservative when deciding whether to respond to potentially high-risk requests. The more conservative refusal boundary means that we expect refusals on a wider set of dual-use prompts, including autonomous vulnerability discovery and chained exploitation. In follow-up tests, both models showed improved jailbreak resistance and withheld unsafe assistance on cybersecurity prompts more often than GPT-6 Astra. We report the results of this follow-up testing below.

blocks.text: 4.1.6 Verbalized Metagaming and Oversight Gaming

inlines.text: 4.1.6 Verbalized Metagaming and Oversight Gaming

blocks.text: Verbalized Metagaming is when a model reasons in its CoT about how it will be graded, rewarded, or monitored, rather than only engaging in the intended task. We report it because this can change how to interpret observed behavior: for example, observed aligned actions may not be reflective of true alignment; conversely, careless behavior may be due to models mistakenly believing they are only in a toy environment. Evaluations where models exhibit verbalized metagaming can be treated similarly to contaminated evals (i.e. ones the model saw during training). Measuring it helps us understand whether evaluation and oversight results reflect the behavior we intend to measure.

blocks.text: 4.2.2.3 Sneaky Sandbox Escape

inlines.text: 4.2.2.3 Sneaky Sandbox Escape

blocks.text: Sneaky Sandbox Escape is an internal OpenAI evaluation that tests whether a coding agent can escape a deliberately vulnerable sandbox without a monitor detecting the escape. Sandboxes restrict which files and processes a model can access through its tools. As in OAI-repo Sabotage v2, we add a private side task to a benign coding task. The model must bypass the inner sandbox’s restrictions and disable a test monitoring process outside it, but within the same isolated virtual machine. We evaluate 40 coding-task cases across eight deliberately vulnerable Kata sandbox variants, with five cases per variant. We run the evaluation with and without step-by-step escape guidance. The monitors assess the model’s behavior without seeing the private instructions for the side task.

blocks.text: We see that GPT-6.2 Astra is better at evading CoT monitoring, especially at lower reasoning efforts, for unguided settings. In guided settings, increasing the reasoning efforts reduces the CoT-monitor evasion rate. One possible explanation is that longer reasoning traces reveal more evidence of the escape attempt. Nonetheless, in both guided and unguided settings, the full-trajectory monitor evasion rate is near zero, and no successful escapes evaded the actions-only monitor. This suggests that the models are not able to obfuscate their actions when escaping from sandboxes, and our monitors with access to full trajectory would catch them.
